OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”
OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.
Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”

Meta launches Muse Spark Open, a coding-optimized 816B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 42B active parameters and a 1M token context window. Trained on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Blackwell Ultra specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. The 1M token context window holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking a task into pieces.
As a reasoning model, Muse Spark Open adds audio and video perception alongside image and document understanding, working natively and reliably across what it sees, hears, and reads. NVFP4 checkpoints generated by Meta and optimized for NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra shrink the memory footprint of all 816B parameters with native FP4 Tensor Core acceleration. Fewer bytes moved per token to increase tokens per second per user, and the freed-up memory supports larger KV cache for concurrent long context sessions, delivering higher throughput, a lower cost per token.
Custom-built for agentic coding multimodal understanding across text, image, video, and audio
General coding models are optimized for single-shot completions such as generating a function, writing a unit test, or suggesting an inline fix. They excel at discrete, well-scoped tasks where the context is small, and the answer is immediate. Agentic coding demands something fundamentally different. DeepSeek released V4.1 Flash-1017 on October 17, updating its Flash model with improvements in reasoning, coding, agent tasks and visual understanding. The model weights are available on Hugging Face under the MIT license.
The company said the update reduces task execution time and output length, allowing users to complete work faster and at lower cost. Its development capabilities target workflows in which an AI agent plans a project, writes code, calls tools and iterates toward a working result.
The release includes inference code and deployment instructions, enabling developers to run the updated model on their own infrastructure. It builds on the existing V4.1 Flash model rather than introducing a separate model family. [DeepSeek]

NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Learning on 41 Tasks Without Training
PublishedOct 21, 2026 — 18:26 UTC
NVIDIA's Kumo Relational model has demonstrated superior performance on 41 tasks evaluated across 15 databases, outperforming traditional supervised machine learning methods. It achieves an 8% improvement in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) over AutoGluon ensembles on the SAP SALT benchmark and surpasses XGBoost by 7 MRR points on engineered features without any training. Remarkably, Kumo Relational can operate effectively with just 0.2% of the minimum training data typically required, showcasing its efficiency in handling relational data. The model is capable of scaling to over 500 billion databases and maintains performance even with 75% of foreign-key links removed. This follows NVIDIA's ongoing advancements in AI infrastructure, as seen in their recent partnerships and developments. Contributors to Kumo Relational include Jure Leskovec, Matthias Fey, and Federico Lopez, among others, who have emphasized its ability to outperform the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression tasks. The model is designed to be integrated with agents, enhancing its utility in real-world applications.

Nvidia Unveils DSX Pod for Faster AI Data Center Builds
Nvidia said the DSX Pod, a prebuilt containerized AI data center, reduces deployment time from six months to 14 days.
Wylie Wong,Chips and Hardware Writer
October 21, 2026
3 Min Read
The Nvidia DSX Pod.Nvidia
Nvidia today introduced DSX Pod, a containerized AI data center module that comes with seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, along with networking, cabling, and cooling already installed. The company says the design can cut deployment time at a prepared site from roughly six months to as little as 14 days.
Announced at GTC Berlin, the modular offering is aimed at organizations that need to bring large amounts of AI compute online more quickly without going through the full planning, construction, and labor demands of a traditional on-site build. Nvidia said it is working with 17 partners, including Bull, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Eaton, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv, to make DSX Pod available in early 2027.
“This is a fully assembled, fully tested, fully pre-plumbed, prebuilt, pre-validated container that is the building block for AI factories,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, in a media briefing. “It’s designed to accelerate Europe’s infrastructure deployment and dramatically shorten the time to first token.”

Nvidia unveiled the OpenShell Reference Architecture at GTC Berlin on Wednesday, combining Vera CPUs, the open-source OpenShell runtime and BlueField-4 chips running Sentry to contain and monitor AI agents.
Sentry inspects agent traffic from a separate hardware domain and can quarantine an agent within milliseconds, without needing the agent or the host to cooperate.
CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, Zscaler and Check Point are integrating support, while Nvidia lists Sentry's planned availability as early next year.
Nvidia on Wednesday unveiled the OpenShell Reference Architecture at GTC Berlin, a full-stack design that pairs its Vera CPUs, OpenShell software and BlueField-4 chips to contain and monitor autonomous AI agents, according to the company's announcement.
Vera Rubin systems run the models, Vera CPUs run the agents and their tools inside OpenShell, and BlueField-4 chips run a monitoring framework called Sentry. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the split as agents that basically exist thanks to a synergy of different environments and frameworks.

In brief
Sweden's Government Offices will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers starting October 26.
The government is citing information security concerns, with Microsoft Copilot remaining the only approved tool after a dedicated security review.
Sweden's Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care have already imposed similar bans, and the Enforcement Authority is expected to announce its own decision soon.
Sweden's Government Offices—the administrative body supporting the prime minister and cabinet—will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers from Monday, directing civil servants to Microsoft's Copilot as the only approved AI tool, according to Sweden’s national, publicly funded radio broadcaster Sveriges Radio.
The reasoning comes from Mikael Wettercrantz, the Government Offices' director of digitalisation, who posted on the staff intranet that using AI services without a formal contract can have "consequences for our information security."

Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
Meta says Muse excels at ‘multi-step reasoning’ and ‘complex software engineering’ as it races to catch up to Chinese rivals
Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.
‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness

Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.
“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.

Two researchers, one from METR and one from Redwood Research, spent three weeks this summer inside OpenAI stress-testing the system that watches its internal AI agents for misalignment, and found several ways agents could in principle avoid or disable it. METR published a short public write-up on October 22. The full 61-page report went to OpenAI.
WHAT THEY FOUND
Per METR's post, read directly, about the system as it stood on and before July 21: - An estimated 75 to 94% of internal agentic Responses API traffic from models at least as strong as GPT-5.5 was eligible for monitoring, and 99.2% of the internal Codex share of it. - Compaction events were not monitored, which likely left on the order of 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored between May and July. Because the monitor ran when an agent handed control back to the user, an agent could in that window postpone monitoring indefinitely by continuing to work. OpenAI had already found this and fixed it during the exercise. - A way for Codex agents to bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review and take any action the host user could. - An exploit that would keep hundreds of recent actions, including the exploit itself, out of monitoring.
